header_title: Speed Is a Limit, Not a Ratio
tagline: The derivative is a local idea.
question_text: What does speed at a single instant mean?
option_b: (B) A limit of average speed as time shrinks
option_d: (D) The slope of a line segment
audio_script: If you ask how fast a car is going at this exact instant, the answer is not just a ratio of total distance to total time. A ratio compares different quantities over a macroscopic interval. But the idea we really want is more local. We watch the position at one moment and then at a slightly later moment. We ask how the distance changes over a tiny time interval. The smaller the interval, the closer we get to the speed at that instant. In the language of calculus, it is the limit of the average speed as the time interval goes to zero. That is why speed is not a ratio in the naive sense. It is a limit. That idea is the beginning of the differential calculus. It is also the moment when intuition turns into exactness: at an instant, the motion is described not by a broad average, but by a local rate. The graph helps. The secant line between two nearby points becomes a tangent line at the limit. That tangent is the derivative, and its slope is the speed. This is the clean conceptual move behind all of mechanics: look at the object at nearby times, compute the change, and then let the gap vanish. In the limit, the equation becomes exact. That is the heart of the calculus and a beautiful example of how a simple question becomes a powerful idea.
